section.title: The Writing on the Wall
section.sectionRationale: A generation after Nebuchadnezzar, his successor Belshazzar throws a drunken feast and desecrates the temple vessels to toast his idols. A disembodied hand writes four words on the wall, and only Daniel can read the verdict: the king has been weighed and found wanting, his kingdom numbered and finished. That very night Babylon falls. It is the sober counterpart to chapter 4, pride that will not learn, judged without reprieve.
section.thesis: The God who holds every ruler's breath in His hand weighs Belshazzar, who defied the Lord of heaven and would not humble himself as his father had, and finds him wanting; the writing on the wall announces a kingdom numbered, weighed, and divided, and that very night Babylon falls.
section.frameNote: Five beats: Belshazzar's feast and the desecration of the temple vessels; the terrifying hand and the wise men's failure; Daniel confronts the king's pride; the inscription read, numbered, weighed, divided; and Babylon falls that very night.

units.label: Belshazzar's feast and the temple vessels

verses.text: Later, King Belshazzar held a great feast for a thousand of his nobles, and he drank wine with them.

Under the influence of the wine, Belshazzar gave orders to bring in the gold and silver vessels that Nebuchadnezzar his father had taken from the temple in Jerusalem, so that the king could drink from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines.
Thus they brought in the gold vessels that had been taken from the temple, the house of God in Jerusalem, and the king drank from them, along with his nobles, his wives, and his concubines.
As they drank the wine, they praised their gods of gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone.

units.label: The terrifying hand on the wall
units.note: the wise men cannot read it

verses.text: At that moment the fingers of a human hand appeared and wrote on the plaster of the wall, near the lampstand in the royal palace. As the king watched the hand that was writing,
his face grew pale and his thoughts so alarmed him that his hips gave way and his knees knocked together.

The king called out for the enchanters, astrologers, and diviners to be brought in, and he said to these wise men of Babylon, “Whoever reads this inscription and tells me its interpretation will be clothed in purple and have a gold chain placed around his neck, and he will be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.”
So all the king's wise men came in, but they could not read the inscription or interpret it for him.
Then King Belshazzar became even more terrified, his face grew even more pale, and his nobles were bewildered.
Hearing the outcry of the king and his nobles, the queen entered the banquet hall. “O king, may you live forever!” she said. “Do not let your thoughts terrify you, or your face grow pale.

There is a man in your kingdom who has the spirit of the holy gods in him. In the days of your father he was found to have insight, intelligence, and wisdom like that of the gods. Your father, King Nebuchadnezzar, appointed him chief of the magicians, enchanters, astrologers, and diviners. Your own father, the king,

did this because Daniel, the one he named Belteshazzar, was found to have an extraordinary spirit, as well as knowledge, understanding, and the ability to interpret dreams, explain riddles, and solve difficult problems. Summon Daniel, therefore, and he will give you the interpretation.”

units.label: Daniel confronts the king's pride
units.note: you did not humble your heart

verses.text: So Daniel was brought before the king, who asked him, “Are you Daniel, one of the exiles my father the king brought from Judah?
I have heard that the spirit of the gods is in you, and that you have insight, intelligence, and extraordinary wisdom.
Now the wise men and enchanters were brought before me to read this inscription and interpret it for me, but they could not give its interpretation.

But I have heard about you, that you are able to give interpretations and solve difficult problems. Therefore, if you can read this inscription and give me its interpretation, you will be clothed in purple and have a gold chain placed around your neck, and you will be made the third highest ruler in the kingdom.”
In response, Daniel said to the king, “You may keep your gifts for yourself and give your rewards to someone else. Nevertheless, I will read the inscription for the king and interpret it for him.
As for you, O king, the Most High God gave your father Nebuchadnezzar sovereignty and greatness, glory and honor.

Because of the greatness that He bestowed on him, the people of every nation and language trembled in fear before him. He killed whom he wished and kept alive whom he wished; he exalted whom he wished and humbled whom he wished.
But when his heart became arrogant and his spirit was hardened with pride, he was deposed from his royal throne, and his glory was taken from him.

He was driven away from mankind, and his mind was like that of a beast. He lived with the wild donkeys and ate grass like an ox, and his body was drenched with the dew of heaven until he acknowledged that the Most High God rules over the kingdom of mankind, setting over it whom He wishes.
But you his son, O Belshazzar, have not humbled your heart, even though you knew all this.

Instead, you have exalted yourself against the {{mare_shemayya|Lord of heaven}}. The vessels from His house were brought to you, and as you drank wine from them with your nobles, wives, and concubines, you praised your gods of silver and gold, bronze and iron, wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or understand. But you have failed to glorify the God who holds in His hand your very breath and all your ways.
Therefore He sent the hand that wrote the inscription.
Now this is the inscription that was written: MENE, MENE, TEKEL, PARSIN.
And this is the interpretation of the message: {{mene|MENE}} means that God has numbered the days of your reign and brought it to an end.
{{tekel|TEKEL}} means that you have been weighed on the scales and found deficient.
{{peres|PERES}} means that your kingdom has been divided and given over to the Medes and Persians.”

units.label: Babylon falls that very night
units.note: the kingdom passes to the Medes

verses.text: Then Belshazzar gave the command, and they clothed Daniel in purple, placed a gold chain around his neck, and proclaimed him the third highest ruler in the kingdom.
That very night Belshazzar king of the Chaldeans was slain,
and Darius the Mede received the kingdom at the age of sixty-two.

mare_shemayya.gloss: The Lord of heaven. Daniel charges that Belshazzar has exalted himself against the Lord of heaven, the God who holds the king's very breath in His hand. The title exposes the folly of the feast: the man toasting idols with holy cups is defying the God who owns his next breath.

mene.gloss: Numbered. Mene sounds like the Aramaic for numbered; it means God has numbered the days of Belshazzar's reign and brought it to an end. The doubling, mene, mene, underlines the certainty of the verdict: the count is finished.

tekel.gloss: Weighed. Tekel sounds like the Aramaic for weighed; the king has been weighed on the scales and found deficient. It is the image of God's judgment testing a life and finding it wanting, a picture that runs throughout Scripture.

peres.gloss: Divided. Peres, the singular of Parsin, sounds like the Aramaic both for divided and for Persia; the kingdom is divided and handed to the Medes and Persians. In one word the verdict names both the sentence and the conqueror who will carry it out that very night.

basic.context: Belshazzar, ruling Babylon a generation after Nebuchadnezzar, throws a lavish drunken feast and, in defiance, drinks toasts to his idols from the sacred cups looted from God's temple. Suddenly a human hand appears and writes on the wall. Terrified, and with his wise men helpless, the king summons Daniel, who refuses the rewards, rebukes his pride, and reads the verdict: God has numbered, weighed, and divided his kingdom. That same night Babylon falls and Belshazzar is killed.
basic.hermeneutics: This narrative is the dark mirror of chapter 4. Nebuchadnezzar was humbled and restored; Belshazzar, who knew the story and refused to learn it, is judged without reprieve. The desecration of the temple vessels shows sin as open contempt for God. The message is that God patiently warns, but pride that will not humble itself finally meets a night when the account is settled.
basic.originalLanguages: Daniel says the king has defied the mare shemayya, the Lord of heaven, who holds his breath. The writing spells out the sentence in Aramaic terms: mene, numbered; tekel, weighed; peres, divided, a word that also sounds like Persia, naming the very conqueror at the gate.
basic.typology: The scales that weigh Belshazzar and find him wanting picture the judgment every person faces before God. Against that verdict, Christ is the one who was weighed and found perfect, and who bears the deficiency of His people, so that all who are in Him are not found wanting on the day of reckoning.
basic.christ: The writing on the wall is a preview of the final judgment, when every life is numbered and weighed. Belshazzar is found deficient; so would we all be. But Jesus stood in our place, fully righteous, and took our sentence, so that those who trust Him are covered by His worth. The God who holds our breath became flesh to give us His life.
basic.god: God is the Lord of heaven who holds every ruler's breath and all his ways in His hand. He is patient, giving warning after warning, but He is also just, and there comes a night when the numbered days run out. He humbles the proud who will not humble themselves, and He hands kingdoms to whom He wills.
basic.crossReferences: Proverbs 16 warns that pride precedes a fall. Galatians 6 says God is not mocked; we reap what we sow. And Hebrews 9 reminds us that it is appointed for man to die once, and after that the judgment, the reality behind the scales.
basic.oneStory: Babylon, the great enemy of God's people, falls in a single night, weighed and found wanting. The God who numbers the days of kingdoms is moving history toward the day when every account is settled and His own kingdom stands. For those in Christ, weighed and yet accepted in Him, that day is not terror but hope.

context.literary:
Chapter 5 is the shortest hinge in the Aramaic half of Daniel, and it is built as a pair with chapter 4. There a king was warned in a dream, wrote his own testimony, and ended by praising God, Daniel 4:34-37. Here a king is warned by a hand, never writes a word, and is dead by the last verse. Daniel 5:18-21 retells chapter 4 in four verses, as though the narrator were handing the lesson back to a man who has already been taught it, and verse 22 delivers the charge: 'you knew all this.'

The scene is a study in reversals. The chapter opens with a thousand nobles and goes on to a room that holds only a terrified king, a fading wall and one old prophet. The man who gives the orders at the start, verse 2, is the man who cannot control his own legs by verse 6. The wise men, who were summoned in every earlier chapter and always failed, fail again, but this time nobody is spared by a clever interpreter's rescue of the guild. Daniel, offered purple and gold in verse 7, refuses them in verse 17, and then receives them anyway in verse 29. The honour is given by a king whose reign has hours left, and the narrator lets the irony stand.

The text keeps a steady rhythm of repetition. The vessels are named three times in the first three verses, the gods of 'gold and silver, bronze and iron, wood and stone' in verse 4 are repeated in verse 23, and the king's pale face and trembling are described in verses 6, 9 and 10. The inscription itself is given twice, bare in verse 25 and then in three explained lines in verses 26 to 28. The final two verses are as terse as a headline, and Daniel's own name is missing from them. The story ends on a king killed and a kingdom passed on, and the reader is left to supply the verdict.
context.historical:
Belshazzar is known from cuneiform records as the son of Nabonidus, the last king of Babylon, who spent long years away from the capital in the Arabian oasis of Tema. In that absence Belshazzar was entrusted with the kingship in Babylon, which fits the odd offer of the 'third highest ruler' in verses 7, 16 and 29: Nabonidus was first, Belshazzar second, and a successful interpreter could be third. The word translated 'father' in verses 2, 11 and 18 can also mean ancestor or predecessor in Hebrew and Aramaic, and 'son' in verse 22 is used in the same broad way, so the narrator speaks of Nebuchadnezzar as the great founder of the house.

Babylon fell in October 539 BC. Ancient sources, including the Babylonian chronicle of Nabonidus and the Greek historians, report that Cyrus took the city with very little fighting. Greek writers add that the river was diverted and the army entered by the bed of the Euphrates while the city was celebrating, which matches the mood of a feast, though Daniel does not describe the method. A thousand nobles at a banquet fits a court that believed the walls made it safe. Isaiah 47:7-9 had told Babylon that she said 'I will be queen forever' and that ruin would come in a single day, and Jeremiah had foretold that her princes and wise men would be made drunk and 'fall asleep forever,' Jeremiah 51:57.

The use of the temple vessels was an act with a long history behind it. Nebuchadnezzar had carried them off and placed them in the treasury of his god, Daniel 1:2, and Jeremiah 27:16-22 warned that false prophets promised a quick return of them while God had said the exile would be long. To drink to idols from these cups was to say that the gods of Babylon had defeated the God of Israel. Cyrus would return the same vessels within a few years, Ezra 1:7.
context.canonical:
The chapter stands inside a long prophetic tradition about Babylon's fall. Isaiah 13:17 names the Medes as the instrument of God's judgment on the city, Isaiah 21:5 pictures a banquet table laid out just before the watchmen are told to rise up, and Isaiah 44:28 to 45:1 names Cyrus as the shepherd and anointed one through whom the exile will end. Jeremiah promised that the nations would serve Babylon only 'until the time of his own land comes,' Jeremiah 27:7, and Jeremiah 25:12 set a limit of seventy years. Daniel 5 is the moment those promises are cashed.

The wall also looks back to the Torah. The only other places where God's writing is described are the tablets 'inscribed by the finger of God,' Deuteronomy 9:10, and the plague that made the magicians confess 'This is the finger of God,' Exodus 8:19. Pharaoh's court and Belshazzar's court share a failure of their wise men before a sign they cannot read. The charge that idols 'cannot see or hear or understand,' Daniel 5:23, echoes Psalm 115:5-7 and the prophets' mockery of Bel and Nebo, Isaiah 46:1.

The New Testament carries the pattern forward. Jesus told of the rich man whose life was required of him 'this very night,' Luke 12:20. Herod in Acts 12:23 is struck down at the moment he accepts praise that belongs to God. And Revelation makes Babylon the standing symbol of every proud world power: 'Fallen, fallen is Babylon the great,' Revelation 14:8 and 18:2, with a golden cup in her hand, Revelation 17:4, and judgment arriving 'in a single hour,' Revelation 18:10. Daniel 5 is the original of that scene.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The first hearers of this chapter were exiles, or the children of exiles, who had grown up beside the empire that had burned their city and carried off their sacred things. They had every reason to suspect that Babylon was too strong to fall and that its gods had proved the stronger. The author tells the story to break that spell. The empire's last feast, with the holy cups raised in praise of lifeless idols, is shown as the exact point at which God acts, and the whole thing is over by morning.

He also wants them to see why. Daniel does not charge Belshazzar with ignorance. He charges him with knowing the lesson of his predecessor and declining to learn it, Daniel 5:22. The real sin is not a mistake about facts but a refusal to humble the heart, and that is a charge that any listener, Babylonian or Israelite, could hear as addressed to themselves.

The author means to give the exiles a model as well. Daniel has no interest in the king's gifts, speaks plainly to a frightened and dangerous man, and then accepts the honours without letting them change what he has said. A people living under foreign power were being shown how to serve a court without belonging to it, and how to tell the truth to power without hatred or flattery.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The chapter records what God did to one king on one night. It does not give a method for reading messages in unexplained events, and it gives no licence to declare that a particular modern ruler has been weighed and found lacking. Daniel reads the writing only because God gave him the interpretation, and the author is careful to say that the wise men could not do it by skill.

What does carry across is the way the story judges Belshazzar. His sin is described with precision: he knew, he did not humble his heart, he used what was holy to honour what was empty, and he gave no glory to the God who held his breath. Those are charges that Scripture presses on every age, and Paul and Peter apply the same logic to the church, Romans 3:23 and 1 Peter 5:5. Daniel's own conduct is also instructive, because he tells the truth without cruelty and without taking what he has refused. Nothing in the story commands us to expect sudden judgment, but it does warn us that delay is not the same as pardon.

debates.question: Who is Darius the Mede who received the kingdom?

views.label: A throne name or governor under Cyrus
views.case: Since no king named Darius the Mede is otherwise attested at this moment, many identify him with a figure such as Gubaru, the governor Cyrus set over Babylon, or take Darius as a throne name or title for a ruler acting under Cyrus, harmonizing the account with the Persian conquest.

views.label: Another name for Cyrus himself
views.case: Some read Daniel 6:28 as saying Daniel prospered in the reign of Darius, that is, the reign of Cyrus, treating Darius the Mede and Cyrus the Persian as the same ruler under two names, a known ancient practice.

debates.bearing: The precise identification is a genuine historical question held with humility; either way the book's point stands, that Babylon fell exactly as God declared and the kingdom passed to the Medes and Persians.

debates.question: Was Belshazzar the son of Nebuchadnezzar?

views.label: Son in a broad sense, the royal line
views.case: Babylonian records name Nabonidus as Belshazzar's father. Hebrew and Aramaic have no separate words for grandfather or predecessor, and the Aramaic words for father and son are used of ancestors and successors. On this reading Belshazzar descends from Nebuchadnezzar's house, perhaps through his mother, and Daniel speaks of the founder of the dynasty as 'father.'

views.label: A literary shorthand for succession
views.case: Others hold that the chapter is not interested in bloodlines but in succession and in the lesson passed down the throne, which is why the mention of the lesson in verse 22 is so sharp. The text pairs the two kings so that the later one can be measured against the earlier, whatever their exact relation.

debates.bearing: Neither view touches the point of the chapter. Whatever the family tree, Belshazzar occupies the throne Nebuchadnezzar held, has the same warning before him, and is answerable for it.

study.originalLanguages:
The chapter is a tangle of verbal play, and most of it is lost in English. The first is the king's body and Daniel's gift. In verse 6 the king's hips 'gave way', and the Aramaic speaks of the joints or knots of his loins being loosened. When the queen and the king later describe Daniel's skill in verses 12 and 16 they say he can 'solve difficult problems,' and the Aramaic there speaks of loosing knots, using the same verb family. The man whose own knots come undone in terror sends for the man who undoes knots. The scene has a quiet comic edge: the king cannot tie himself together, and the interpreter's whole craft is to untie.

The word for interpretation, pesher, appears again and again in this chapter, in verses 7, 8, 12, 15, 16, 17 and 26, as the word the king wants and the wise men cannot supply. It is related to the verb meaning to loosen or solve, and so it fits the knots. In Daniel 5, interpretation is not guessing but the releasing of a message that God has bound.

The three words of the sentence are measures as well as verbs. Mene is from a root meaning to count or number, tekel from a root meaning to weigh, and parsin the plural of peres, from a root meaning to divide or break. Many scholars notice that the words can also be heard as nouns for weights, a mina, a shekel, and half-units, as if a rate of exchange had been written on the wall: the great King's valuation of a lesser one. The doubling of mene in verse 25 is not explained in verses 26 to 28, where each word is explained once, but a doubled word elsewhere in Scripture signals certainty, as when Joseph says that a doubled dream means 'the matter has been decreed by God,' Genesis 41:32. Daniel also changes the form of the third word, from parsin in verse 25 to peres in verse 28, so the pun on Persia can be heard in the singular name of the conqueror.

The word for 'deficient' in verse 27 is from a root meaning to lack. Daniel does not say that Belshazzar was wicked in the abstract, but that he was weighed 'on the scales' and found short. The scale of Scripture is God's, and He is the one who weighs motives, Proverbs 16:2, and by whom actions are weighed, 1 Samuel 2:3. In Psalm 62:9 even the exalted, weighed on the scale, are lighter than a breath.

Verse 26 says that God 'brought it to an end.' The verb is built on the same root as shalom and shalem, meaning to complete. God does not merely cut the reign short; He finishes it, as a task is finished. And in verse 23 the charge is that Belshazzar failed to glorify the God who holds his 'breath,' the Aramaic cousin of the word neshamah used in Genesis 2:7 for the breath of life. The king's very ability to give an order at the feast was a loan from the God he insulted.

Finally, in verse 22 the verb of the charge, 'you have not humbled,' is from the root shpl, to be low, the same root heard in Daniel 4:37, where Nebuchadnezzar says that God 'is able to humble those who walk in pride.' The son is charged with refusing what the father was made to learn.

typology.type: The holy vessels used for idol worship, Daniel 5:2-4
typology.fulfillment: The cups were set apart for the service of the LORD, and Belshazzar uses them for a toast to gods of wood and stone. The pattern is that what belongs to God cannot be taken for ordinary use without being judged. In Christ the vessels are fulfilled in two ways. His own body is the true temple, John 2:19-21, and He promises to raise it. And believers, whose bodies are 'a temple of the Holy Spirit,' 1 Corinthians 6:19, are called to be 'vessels for honor,' 2 Timothy 2:20-21. The type falls short because the gold cups could be stolen and abused, but the temple of Christ's body was given up by His own will and raised in power.

typology.type: Purple and a gold chain, the court's honour, Daniel 5:29
typology.fulfillment: Daniel is dressed in purple by a king who will be dead before dawn. It is an honour with no future behind it. The Gospels set a deliberate contrast, for the soldiers dressed Jesus in a purple robe and twisted a crown of thorns, Mark 15:17 and John 19:2, mocking a man they thought powerless. Where Belshazzar's honour is empty and his kingdom is about to be divided, the mockery of Jesus becomes a true coronation, since He is the King whose kingdom 'will never be destroyed, nor will it be left to another people,' Daniel 2:44. The type is an echo of irony, not a direct prophecy.

typology.type: The hand that writes on the wall, Daniel 5:5
typology.fulfillment: A human hand appears and writes a decree that only God can explain. Throughout Scripture writing is how God makes a verdict permanent, from the tablets written by the finger of God, Deuteronomy 9:10, to the ledger of debt that stood against us. In Christ that written record is dealt with. God cancelled 'the debt ascribed to us in the decrees that stood against us,' and 'nailed it to the cross,' Colossians 2:14. The writing on the wall was a sentence handed to one man; the cross is the place where the sentence against many was taken and paid. The type is partial, because Belshazzar's verdict was carried out, while ours was carried by another.

typology.type: The scroll no one can read, Daniel 5:8 and Revelation 5:3-5
typology.fulfillment: The wise men stand before an inscription they cannot read, and only God's chosen servant can give its meaning. In the last book of the Bible the same scene returns on a cosmic scale: a scroll in God's hand which 'no one in heaven or on earth or under the earth was able to open,' until the Lion of the tribe of Judah 'has triumphed to open the scroll,' Revelation 5:3-5. Daniel is a servant who reads what God has written; Christ is the one who is worthy to carry it out. The pattern is real, but Daniel merely announces the verdict, while Christ executes the purposes of God.

study.christ:
This chapter leads to Christ most plainly by contrast. Belshazzar, offered a lesson in the form of his father's humbling, refused it. The Son of God, by contrast, 'learned obedience from what He suffered,' Hebrews 5:8, and did what Belshazzar would not: He humbled Himself. Daniel's charge to the king, 'you have not humbled your heart,' is answered in the New Testament by Philippians 2:8, where Christ humbles Himself to death on a cross, and by the promise that whoever humbles himself will be exalted, Matthew 23:12. The throne of Babylon fell because its king would not stoop; the throne of Christ was won because its King did.

It leads to Christ by the figure of the scales. Belshazzar was weighed and found short. Every human being faces the same measure, for all 'fall short of the glory of God,' Romans 3:23, and the hand on the wall is a picture of a verdict already written. The gospel does not tear the scale down. It says that one person has been weighed and was found complete. Pilate, the Roman governor, said of Jesus, 'I find no basis for a charge against this man,' Luke 23:4, and Hebrews says He was tempted in every way yet 'without sin,' Hebrews 4:15. At the cross He was made 'to be sin on our behalf, so that in Him we might become the righteousness of God,' 2 Corinthians 5:21. Paul's great desire is to 'be found in Him, not having my own righteousness,' Philippians 3:9, which is the answer to the word found in verse 27: found lacking in oneself, found complete in Christ. The result is that 'there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus,' Romans 8:1.

It leads to Christ through the scroll motif. In Daniel the wise men cannot read the inscription and one man must be found who can. In Revelation 5:3-5 no one is found worthy to open God's scroll until the Lion of Judah comes forward. Daniel read the verdict; Christ carries out the whole plan of God.

And it leads to Him by the kingdom. Belshazzar's kingdom 'has been divided,' verse 28, and given to others. Daniel 2:44 promises a kingdom that will not 'be left to another people,' and Hebrews 12:28 says that those in Christ are 'receiving an unshakable kingdom.' Babylon ends in one night; Christ's kingdom has no night.

A caution is needed. The chapter is not a code in which each detail points to Jesus; the feast, the lampstand and the chain are not symbols to be decoded. The links above rest on the way the New Testament itself uses this pattern of judgment, humility and the weighing of a life, and on the larger contrast between the kingdoms of the earth and the kingdom Daniel says God will set up.
study.god:
The chapter shows a God who sees what no one else notices. At the feast, no one is asked to read the heart of the king. God sees it, and sends the hand 'at that moment,' verse 5, when the cups are lifted. The Lord of heaven is not an absentee. He sits within the banquet hall, and every drink raised to an idol is raised before Him.

He is patient, and the patience is documented. Daniel 5:18 to 21 is a summary of what God had already done, a whole chapter's worth of warning, and verse 22 says that the king had known it. The judgment of this chapter is not sudden in God's account. It follows a lesson that had been available for a generation. At the same time, patience has an end. 'Therefore He sent the hand,' verse 24, is the word of a God who has waited and now acts. The Bible does not allow us to treat the delay of judgment as a sign that God does not judge.

He is the God who gives and takes away kingdoms. Daniel 5:18 says that the Most High 'gave your father Nebuchadnezzar sovereignty and greatness, glory and honor.' Everything that Belshazzar had was a gift. Daniel 4:35 declares that no one can restrain His hand. This holds together two truths the chapter does not soften: God uses human powers, like the Medes and Persians who were promised in Isaiah 13:17, and He is not made guilty by what they do. The same hand that gives Babylon's dominion also ends it.

He is the God who weighs. The picture of scales speaks of exactness. Proverbs 16:2 says that motives are weighed out by the LORD, and the word of the wall means that God's accounting is not a matter of rumour or reputation. He measures with a true weight. And He is the God who holds 'your very breath and all your ways,' which means the reign of every ruler is a lease.

He is also the God whose people are not abandoned in a faithless court. Daniel is kept, given a voice, and brought in at the very hour when the king's own experts are exhausted. The God who judges the proud is the God who keeps a record of the faithful, and who raised up one man to say the truth in a hall of drunken nobles.

For worship, the chapter calls us to a reverent fear that is also a relief. It is a fear because God weighs; it is a relief because the empire that frightened Israel is only a lease, and the King who holds our breath is the one who has promised to keep His people.

crossReferences.note: Nebuchadnezzar's own testimony after his humbling. He lifted his eyes to heaven, his sanity returned, and he praised the God who is 'able to humble those who walk in pride.' Belshazzar had this record in his own palace, and Daniel's charge in 5:22 depends on it.

God says He will make Babylon's princes and wise men drunk so that they 'fall asleep forever and not wake up.' The prophecy describes a feast that ends in a sleep from which there is no waking, and it fits the night of Daniel 5:30 exactly.

Isaiah sees a table laid, a carpet spread, the people eating and drinking, and then a cry to the princes to oil their shields. The prophet pictures the same ruin that Daniel tells, a city caught at its dinner, and shows that the fall was announced long before the hand wrote.

The LORD names Cyrus as His anointed, whose right hand He has grasped 'to open the doors before him, so that the gates will not be shut.' God had written the end of Babylon in advance, and Daniel 5:28 names the people into whose hand the kingdom would go.

The psalmist describes idols as having mouths, eyes and ears but being unable to speak, see or hear. Daniel 5:23 uses the same charge against the gods of gold and silver, wood and stone, which cannot see or hear or understand, while the true God sees the feast and sends a hand.

Jesus's parable of the rich man ends with God's words, 'This very night your life will be required of you.' The parallel to Daniel 5:30 is close: a man secure in his possessions, a sudden night, and the question of who will own what he has collected.

The kings of the earth stand at a distance and cry, 'In a single hour your judgment has come.' John uses Babylon as the symbol of every proud empire, and the speed of the fall in Daniel 5 is the pattern for the last collapse of a world that has refused to humble itself.

The scales of verse 27 find every person short. Paul announces the exchange that answers the verdict: God made the sinless Christ to be sin so that 'in Him we might become the righteousness of God.' The deficit that was fatal to Belshazzar is covered for those who are found in Christ.

A written decree stood against us, and God took it away and nailed it to the cross. Where the writing on the wall announced a sentence on one man, the cross is the place where the written charge against many was cancelled.

A man's ways seem pure to him, but 'his motives are weighed out by the LORD.' The proverb states in a line what Daniel 5:27 shows in a scene: the king's self-assessment at the feast counted for nothing, and the only weighing that mattered was God's.

'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble.' James states the principle on which the two kings of Daniel 4 and 5 are judged. One was humbled and restored; the other stayed proud and was overthrown, so the same God gave opposite answers to the same lesson.

study.oneStory:
The chapter belongs to the long conflict between Babylon and the people of God, a conflict that begins at the tower of Babel, Genesis 11:4, where people said they would 'make a name for ourselves.' Babel was the first attempt to build a world without God, and Babylon in Daniel is that attempt at its height. Belshazzar's feast is Babel with a banquet table: the nations gathered, the holy things used for show, and a king who sits in the place of God.

The story answers the exiles' question from before, which is whether the God who allowed Jerusalem to fall had lost to the gods of Babylon. In Daniel 5 the answer comes in the plainest form possible. The vessels that were carried to Babylon are put to use in a toast to those gods, and that night God ends the kingdom that carried them off. The same God who gave Jerusalem into Nebuchadnezzar's hand, Daniel 1:2, takes Babylon from the hand of his successor.

It also sets up what follows. The Medes and Persians receive the kingdom, and in that new reign a faithful man will again face a law written against his God, Daniel 6. Cyrus will return the vessels and send the exiles home, Ezra 1:7, so that the writing on the wall becomes the first step in the return from exile. And the visions of chapters 7 and 8 will place Babylon, Persia and Greece in a sequence that God is writing, empire after empire, with a limit set to each.

The Bible continues to use Babylon as a type. In Revelation 14:8, 17:4 and 18:2 the name is applied to the world system that makes the nations drunk with its wine and uses holy things for gain, and its fall is announced with the same words that Daniel's night implied. What Daniel 5 does in one night, Revelation 18 does for the world: 'in a single hour your judgment has come,' Revelation 18:10.

In the new creation there is no Babylon and no scale left hanging in suspense. The kingdom that is 'unshakable,' Hebrews 12:28, belongs to the Lamb, and the people who were found in Him come with no deficit. Revelation 21 describes a city whose gates are never shut, with no night there. The hall where a king's face turned pale is replaced by a city where God's people look at His face and live.

quiz.q: What act of defiance marked Belshazzar's feast?

options.text: He drank toasts to his idols from the sacred vessels looted from God's temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: Daniel 5:2-4 shows the deliberate sacrilege that provokes the judgment.

options.text: He simply held a large banquet with much wine.
options.note: The feast was real, but the offense was desecrating the holy temple vessels to praise idols.

options.text: He refused to invite the wise men of Babylon.
options.note: The wise men were summoned later; the offense was the sacrilege with the vessels.

options.text: He tore down the temple in Jerusalem.
options.note: The temple had been plundered earlier; here he abuses the vessels already taken.

quiz.q: Why was Belshazzar more guilty than Nebuchadnezzar had been?

options.text: He knew how God had humbled his father, yet still refused to humble his own heart.
options.note: Daniel 5:22 makes his knowledge the aggravating factor.

options.text: He committed more feasts than his father.
options.note: The issue was not the number of feasts but refusing to learn from a known warning.

options.text: He was a foreigner and did not know the true God.
options.note: He did know the story of Nebuchadnezzar, which is why his pride was worse.

options.text: He had never heard of the God of Israel.
options.note: Daniel says he knew all this, so his defiance was willful.

quiz.q: What did the words on the wall mean?

options.text: Numbered, weighed, and divided: God had ended his reign, found him wanting, and given his kingdom to the Medes and Persians.
options.note: Daniel 5:26-28 gives the threefold interpretation.

options.text: A blessing promising a long and prosperous reign.
options.note: The opposite; the words announced judgment and the end of his reign.

options.text: A riddle with no clear meaning.
options.note: Daniel read it plainly as a verdict of judgment.

options.text: A list of the king's treasures.
options.note: They were terms of judgment: numbered, weighed, divided.

quiz.q: How did Daniel respond to the king's offer of rewards?

options.text: He told the king to keep the gifts, then read and interpreted the writing anyway.
options.note: Daniel 5:17 shows his integrity, unbought by the king's rewards.

options.text: He eagerly accepted the purple robe and gold chain first.
options.note: He declined the rewards before speaking, refusing to be bought.

options.text: He refused to speak unless paid double.
options.note: He asked for nothing and spoke the truth freely.

options.text: He fled the palace in fear.
options.note: He stayed and boldly delivered God's verdict.

quiz.q: How does being weighed and found wanting point us to Christ?

options.text: All fall short in God's scales, but Christ was found perfect and bears our deficiency, so those in Him are not condemned.
options.note: The scales picture judgment; Christ is our righteousness, Romans 3:23-24.

options.text: It teaches that good deeds will always outweigh bad ones.
options.note: The point is that we are all found wanting; our hope is Christ's righteousness, not our balance of deeds.

options.text: It shows that only kings are judged by God.
options.note: The scales picture the judgment all people face, not only kings.

options.text: It has no bearing on Christ or salvation.
options.note: The scene previews the judgment from which only Christ can deliver.

questions: Belshazzar treated holy things with contempt to entertain his guests. Where might you be treating what belongs to God casually or carelessly?
He knew the story of his father's humbling but refused to learn from it. What lessons has God already put before you that you are slow to take to heart?
The God who holds your very breath is the one Belshazzar defied. How does remembering that every breath is a gift from God reshape your day?
Daniel could not be bought; he spoke the truth whatever the reward. Where are you tempted to soften God's truth for the sake of approval or gain?
The scales of judgment would find any of us wanting. How does resting in the righteousness of Christ change the way you face the thought of God's judgment?

translationNotes.note: The Aramaic does not include Later; about thirty years have passed since chapter 4, so some translations add many years later to mark the gap.
Father can mean predecessor, ancestor, or grandfather; Belshazzar was a successor of Nebuchadnezzar, ruling as co-regent under his father Nabonidus.
The four words, mene, mene, tekel, parsin, are Aramaic terms that sound like numbered, weighed, and divided; peres, the singular of parsin, also sounds like Persia.
Darius the Mede is variously identified with a governor set over Babylon by Cyrus, or with Cyrus himself under another name; the historical question is held with humility.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched this session from bible.helloao.org for Daniel 5:1-31. Chapter 5 is Aramaic, so load-bearing lexicon entries use Aramaic.
